Yes, the story has an appropriate and effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer skillfully uses summary and exposition at the beginning and end of the story—as well as in brief transitions between days on the cruise—to compress time and provide essential background information (such as the parents' divorce, the father's terminal illness, and his eventual passing). This grounds the reader without bogging down the pacing. 

At the same time, the emotional core of the narrative unfolds through vivid, real-time scenes. Key moments—like the first dinner with the tablemates, meeting Eli at the pool, the argument on the balcony, the first kiss, and the final slow dance between father and daughter—are fully dramatized with sharp dialogue and specific physical actions. This balance allows the story to cover years of emotional history while keeping the reader deeply engaged in the immediate, poignant moments of the seven-day cruise.
